photos.alt: The back face of the 2026 Sydney Marathon finisher medal showing Sydney landmarks including the Opera House and Harbour Bridge — alongside Munich's Allianz Arena diamond-patterned roof.
photos.story: The 2026 Sydney Marathon finisher medal — going to ~40,000 runners — celebrates Sydney's iconic landmarks but accidentally engraved Munich's Allianz Arena instead of Sydney's Allianz Stadium because a designer confused the two Allianz-named venues.
photos.why_funny: Organisers declined to replace the medals and quipped 'We're not going to run from it,' while Munich's Allianz Arena posted: 'Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!'

photos.alt: A grey traffic speed-enforcement camera mounted on a roadside pole, trees in the background
photos.story: Slovakia installed 279 NERO R-ONE speed cameras using EU road-safety funds, then its national security service discovered they were rebranded Russian gear with SMS-triggered backdoor shell access and passwordless live video feeds.
photos.why_funny: A government scheme to make roads safer accidentally handed Russia a ready-to-activate nationwide surveillance network—reachable by a text from a St Petersburg phone number.

photos.alt: Unitree Superman humanoid robot bent sharply in half at the waist after crashing into a padded safety barrier during sprint training for the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, torso folded forward over its legs with sparks at the impact point.
photos.story: Unitree's 'Superman' humanoid robot hit 12.66 m/s during sprint training for the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing — faster than Usain Bolt's peak speed — then couldn't stop and slammed into a safety cushion, snapping completely at the waist in a shower of sparks, one day before the games officially opened.
photos.why_funny: The robot nailed the speed goal and completely failed at the 'not destroying itself upon reaching the end of the track' part, prompting the internet to coin 'first career-ending injury in robotic athletics.'

photos.alt: Murchison Tower at Trinity University in San Antonio — a tall Gothic stone bell tower on the campus skyline.
photos.story: Trinity University unveiled a new sunburst logo on July 30, 2026, replacing the iconic 166-foot Murchison Tower — then paused the entire rollout within five days after alumni flooded social media saying it looked like every hotel and bank logo ever made.
photos.why_funny: After consulting over 300 people for nearly a year, they produced something so generic that the university itself had to hit pause before anyone even ordered new stationery.

photos.alt: Buffalo Bills fans peering over a thick concrete platform labelled 'BRUCE SMITH 78' at the new Highmark Stadium, looking through a glass safety barrier in an attempt to see the field below.
photos.story: The Buffalo Bills opened brand-new Highmark Stadium in August 2026 to viral complaints: fans who paid tens of thousands for Personal Seat Licenses found their $2.2B views blocked by concrete ledges, glass safety barriers, and staircase railings — and the architect called it 'intentional design'.
photos.why_funny: A stadium costing $2.2 billion managed to block paying fans' sightlines with concrete and glass, then the designer said the obstructions were a feature, not a bug.

photos.alt: The back of the Google Pixel 11 Pro being held in a hand, with the HiLight LED array glowing in vivid blue-green hues along the camera bar — the notification lights visible only because the phone is being shown from behind.
photos.story: Google's Pixel 11 Pro (launched August 12, 2026, starting at $1,099) features 'HiLight' — an array of RGB LEDs on the back of the phone that glow to notify you of calls and Gemini AI activity; the fundamental problem, immediately noted by reviewers, is that the lights face away from you and are almost invisible during normal face-up use.
photos.why_funny: A premium smartphone's headline new feature is a notification light placed on the side of the screen you're never looking at, and at launch it only tells you two things: a favourite contact is calling, or the AI is thinking.

photos.alt: The USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78), the lead Ford-class aircraft carrier, photographed at sea near the Solent off the English coast in 2022 — the class whose EMALS electromagnetic launch system is at the centre of the reversal decision
photos.story: On August 13, 2026, Trump signed a directive ordering Ford-class aircraft carriers to replace EMALS — the electromagnetic launch system the Navy spent $4+ billion extra on because steam was 'outdated' — with steam catapults starting from the USS Doris Miller (CVN-81); the catch is that nobody in the US has built a steam catapult in roughly twenty years, the reversal will cost billions more and could delay the carrier from 2034 to the end of the next decade.
photos.why_funny: The US Navy replaced steam catapults with billion-dollar electromagnetic ones because steam was old-fashioned, then ordered the billion-dollar electromagnetic ones replaced with steam because steam is reliable — making both decisions simultaneously correct and catastrophically expensive.

photos.alt: Instagram's 2026 redesigned wordmark displayed in black on a light background, showing the distinctive new lowercase 'r' letterform that closely resembles a 'z'
photos.story: Instagram unveiled its first wordmark redesign in a decade on August 13, 2026, but the stylised lowercase 'r' sits so close to the 'g' that the internet immediately renamed the platform 'Instagzam' — a typography design flaw baked into a global brand refresh used by two billion people.
photos.why_funny: A trillion-dollar company hired designers to update four letters and shipped a logo that mispells the product name at first glance.

photos.alt: The Grokipedia homepage interface — a Wikipedia-style AI-generated encyclopedia launched by Elon Musk's xAI in 2025 — as it appeared before its April 2026 editorial freeze
photos.story: xAI launched Grokipedia in October 2025 as an AI-powered Wikipedia rival that grew to 6 million articles; it stopped updating entirely on April 24, 2026, leaving 13,002 user edits stuck 'in review' for three months — while Musk never mentioned it after February and 6.7 million monthly visitors kept reading its frozen, unmoderated content without any warning.
photos.why_funny: The AI encyclopedia that promised to never go out of date became more out of date than the Encyclopaedia Britannica volumes gathering dust in your parents' garage — and it didn't even tell anyone.

photos.alt: Side-by-side product photo of the HONOR Robot Phone: left panel shows the silver handset back with its mechanical gimbal arm module; right panel shows a close-up of the robotic camera arm fully extended with the square camera module dangling on the articulated titanium arm
photos.story: HONOR launched the Robot Phone on August 12, 2026 — a $1,485 smartphone with a 4-degree-of-freedom titanium robotic arm camera that extends above the screen, tracks subjects, responds to 10 gestures, and dances to music — co-engineered with cinema camera company ARRI, because apparently normal cameras weren't cinematically ambitious enough.
photos.why_funny: The design brief was apparently 'what if the camera was alive?' and the answer was a phone that can nod its tiny titanium head in agreement with you.

photos.alt: Edinburgh North Bridge viewed from street level, showing the grand Victorian stone bridge carrying car traffic across a deep valley, with no cycle lanes or cycling infrastructure visible
photos.story: Edinburgh's North Bridge closed in 2018 for major refurbishment, with plans to create a cycling and public transport corridor; it fully reopened on July 31, 2026 — after eight years — with no cycling infrastructure whatsoever, just regular car lanes, leaving cyclists to navigate around one of the city's busiest crossings exactly as before.
photos.why_funny: Eight years of Edinburgh telling cyclists 'we're working on it' culminated in a grand unveiling of: a road.

photos.alt: Close-up of the front of a Samsung Galaxy Tab S8 Ultra showing the dual front-facing cameras mounted in the V-shaped notch cutout at the top of the display — the same notch design confirmed to continue in the Tab S12 Ultra
photos.story: Leaked renders published August 8–11, 2026 confirmed that the upcoming Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra will keep the exact same V-shaped display notch first introduced on the Tab S8 Ultra in 2022 — a design users have criticised as 'unsightly' for four years — while rivals moved to punch-hole or under-display cameras; tech outlets called it 'our worst fears confirmed.'
photos.why_funny: Samsung spent four years listening to customers beg them to remove the notch from their premium 14.6-inch AMOLED display, then built the exact same notch again and called it a flagship.

photos.alt: Man standing at a Walmart electric vehicle charging station in an outdoor parking lot, no overhead canopy or weather protection visible
photos.story: On August 10, 2026, a viral clip of a man charging his EV at Walmart sparked widespread 'why can't we build chargers with covers?' complaints — Walmart's outdoor charging stations have no overhead canopy, unlike every gas station built in the last century, leaving EV drivers exposed to sun, rain, and snow.
photos.why_funny: The future of transportation promises to be frictionless, yet the reality is standing in the rain next to a pole in a Walmart lot wondering why 1940s gas station designers managed to figure out canopies.

photos.alt: The Ford 'FATHOM' name badge — white letters spelling FATHOM™ on a black rectangular metal plate against a dark textured background — the entire visual announcement for Ford's declared 'Model T moment'
photos.story: Ford CEO Jim Farley announced on August 6, 2026 that the 'Fathom,' a $28,350 electric pickup truck, represents Ford's 'Model T moment' and 'breakthrough electric vehicle' — but the actual truck design won't be revealed until early 2027, so the announcement image is literally just the name badge on a black surface while critics said the compact pickup doesn't address the right market.
photos.why_funny: Ford declared a historic 'Model T moment' for a truck they are not yet allowed to show anyone, which means their generation-defining breakthrough currently looks like a hotel room safe.

photos.alt: Concept render of the OpenAI speaker — a fabric-covered donut/ring shape shown in a hand alongside diagrams labelled Spin, Tilt, and Click, with OpenAI logo and text reading 'Moving parts that help give it personality'
photos.story: OpenAI acquired Jony Ive's design studio for $6.4 billion in 2025, assembled a 200-person hardware team, and unveiled its first product on August 6: a hockey-puck-sized ring speaker with no screen and 'moving parts for personality,' priced at $300–$400 and launching in 2027 — critics immediately compared it to the failed $699 Humane AI Pin.
photos.why_funny: The world's most hyped AI company paid iPhone-designer money to put a hole in a speaker and give it fidget-toy features.

photos.alt: 2026 Audi Q9 SUV photographed from the right-front quarter in daylight, showing the massive Singleframe grille, four-ring badge, and — crucially — perfectly ordinary conventional door handles on a $90,000 car
photos.story: Audi's CEO Gernot Döllner drove the Q9 prototype once with its piezoelectric winglet door handles — which would open via a touch-sensitive flap instead of a conventional lever — decided they were 'worse than a conventional door handle', and ordered an emergency 45-week redesign to put regular door handles back on their upcoming $90,000 flagship SUV, a process that normally takes two years.
photos.why_funny: Audi's proudest engineering achievement for its most expensive SUV is that it successfully put back the thing it spent years trying to remove.

photos.alt: A padlocked metal gate installed across the full width of a marked cycle path in Tower Hamlets, London, with cycle lane markings visible on the ground and the locked gate completely blocking access
photos.story: In August 2026, Tower Hamlets council installed a full-width padlocked gate across a marked, heavily-used cycle path in London, with no alternative route and no key for cyclists — prompting widespread ridicule from residents who called it 'car-brained' planning; cyclists arriving at the gate are forced to turn back or lift their bikes around it, while a standard removable bollard would have blocked cars without stopping cyclists at all.
photos.why_funny: The council chose the most bicycle-hostile possible solution to stop cars from entering a cycle path — accidentally converting an active cycle route into a dead-end.

photos.alt: Ray-Ban Meta Gen 1 smart glasses and their white charging case resting on a surface, looking identical to regular Ray-Ban sunglasses with no visible camera or recording indicators
photos.story: Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses were deliberately designed to be indistinguishable from regular sunglasses so people wouldn't feel judged wearing them; that exact design decision enabled users to secretly film strangers without detection, earning the glasses the nickname 'pervert glasses,' and now legitimate wearers are too scared to wear them in public — Instagram cracked down on covertly-shot videos from the glasses on July 28, 2026.
photos.why_funny: The feature that was supposed to make the glasses socially acceptable — looking completely normal — is the same feature that made them socially radioactive.

photos.alt: Cracker Barrel Old Country Store restaurant exterior in Bloomsburg, Pennsylvania, showing the original red sign, rocking chairs on the porch, and barrels by the entrance — the nostalgic branding management tried and failed to replace.
photos.story: Cracker Barrel CEO Julie Masino unveiled a minimalist wordmark in August 2025, dumping the beloved 'Uncle Herschel' rocking-chair logo; the stock lost $100M in one day, Trump tweeted, and the logo was reversed in six days — then Masino stepped down July 27, 2026, telling Glenn Beck: 'I feel like I've been fired by America.'
photos.why_funny: The CEO hired to modernize America's most aggressively un-modern restaurant chain outlasted her rebrand by exactly one year before being un-modernized herself.

photos.alt: A Foundation Series Tesla Cybertruck photographed at dusk in South San Jose, showing the flat angular stainless steel body, geometric headlight strip, and completely straight panel lines with no visible curves
photos.story: A Bloomberg analysis published July 22, 2026 showed Tesla's Cybertruck is a bigger commercial failure relative to targets than Ford's 1957 Edsel — the historical benchmark for automotive flops — after Musk projected 250,000 annual sales but the truck managed only 3,519 deliveries in Q1 2026 and fewer than 8,000 units through May 2026, with stock falling 18% in a week.
photos.why_funny: The man who promised Tesla's 'best product ever' built a stainless steel truck that looks like a refrigerator tipped on its side and sold it at one-sixth the promised annual rate — to fewer people, proportionally, than even the Edsel.

photos.alt: Chester Cheeks toy product packaging — a round smiling face that is unmistakably shaped from cartoon buttock forms, wearing oversized headphones, shown against colourful product art with the Butt Face logo
photos.story: Goliath Games launched Chester Cheeks worldwide on July 6, 2026 — a $49 interactive toy whose face is literally shaped like cartoon buttocks, which makes fart sounds and dances when children press, squeeze, or spread its cheeks; Australian Big W shoppers found it on July 30 and demanded a recall, with one parent calling it 'very inappropriate indeed' while Goliath markets it as 'perfect for parties and pranks.'
photos.why_funny: The product team looked at a butt, thought 'children's face,' a global toy company approved it, and the only people who weren't in on the joke were the parents at the school-supply aisle.

photos.alt: Screenshot of Google Earth's AI image creation interface showing a prompt-generated futuristic fantasy city with glowing green hyperloop pathways, a massive transparent dome arena, and a spiraling tower, overlaid on real satellite imagery of a city grid, with 'Refine image' and 'Save to project' buttons visible and a disclaimer reading 'Generative AI can make mistakes, so double-check it'
photos.story: On July 31, 2026, Google launched an AI image generation feature for Google Earth that let users prompt-generate fake imagery and superimpose it over real satellite maps; after critics flagged that this gave anyone a tool to fabricate evidence using 'one of the most reliable sources of visual evidence,' Google pulled the feature the following day — while it was live the disclaimer read 'Generative AI can make mistakes, so double-check it.'
photos.why_funny: Google built a way to put photorealistic fake cities on real maps, released it to the public, and then noticed this was a bad idea at exactly the same moment everyone else did.

photos.alt: NYC DOT cross-section diagram of Grand Street showing the proposed layout: two car travel lanes and a parking lane taking 23 feet, with only an 8-foot two-way bike lane squeezed into the remainder
photos.credit: NYC Department of Transportation / Streetsblog NYC
photos.story: New York City's DOT revealed plans for a two-way 'protected' bike lane on Grand Street in Lower Manhattan that is only 8 feet total — 4 feet per direction — less than half the recommended minimum width, while 23 of the street's 34 feet remain allocated to cars including space for double-parking.
photos.why_funny: The city's own planning diagram shows cyclists getting a strip barely wider than a car door while the double-parking lane stays, then called it a 'protected' bike path.

photos.alt: Architectural rendering of seven large stacked boulder-shaped structures rising from Rotterdam's riverbank, rendered as smooth rounded lumps
photos.story: Dutch firm MVRDV won a €240M competition to build Rotterdam's next landmark with 'Rotterdam Rocks!' — seven stacked lumpy boulders on the Maas riverfront — and readers immediately called it 'a bad acid trip' and 'something Shrek would throw up.'
photos.why_funny: An architectural rendering of what is objectively a pile of cartoon boulders, presented to the public as a serious world wonder.

photos.alt: A humanlike Realbotix humanoid robot with realistic silicone skin and facial features stands at the Realbotix booth at CES 2025 in Las Vegas, interacting with attendees
photos.story: Salamanca City Central School District in rural upstate New York approved a $60,000 purchase of a humanlike AI robot named 'Sally' — built by Realbotix, whose sibling company manufactures hyper-realistic adult sex dolls — to teach high school students robotics; state education officials and the teachers union forced the school to pause the pilot after the manufacturer's product line was discovered.
photos.why_funny: The school board vetted the robot's teaching credentials before anyone checked what else the manufacturer makes.

photos.alt: Open PS4 game cases with physical Blu-ray discs visible for The Witcher: Wild Hunt and Call of Duty: Black Ops 6, surrounded by more physical game cases
photos.credit: Stanislav Kogiku/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
photos.story: Sony announced physical PlayStation game disc production ends January 2028 — despite 82% of PS5 consoles sold having disc drives — while simultaneously unveiling a Sony Electronics vinyl turntable for music fans who love physical media.
photos.why_funny: Sony supports physical media in exactly one format: the one PlayStation doesn't use.

photos.alt: The Grind & Unwind café storefront with AI-generated food display photos visible in the window and graffiti on the facade
photos.story: Grind & Unwind café in San Francisco used AI-generated images on their storefront menu that looked like food hallucinated by a model that had never seen food, sparking enough online fury that someone spray-painted 'SERIOUSLY' on the facade — costing the owner $700 to clean.
photos.why_funny: The AI was given one job: make people want to eat here. It produced images that made people want to spray-paint the building.

photos.alt: A huge LED-covered robot costume performer dances at an outdoor community festival with 'Irondale' visible on a sign in the background and a crowd of families watching
photos.story: Irondale, Alabama rebranded its community festival as 'AI Love Irondale Day' to attract tech investment, faced an immediate online backlash calling it 'a pep rally for data centers,' and the mayor reversed course within days — but the festival's AI robot turned out to be a performer in an enormous LED-lit costume dancing in a parking lot.
photos.why_funny: The town promised an AI-powered future and delivered a dude in a very large plastic robot suit doing the Achy Breaky Heart in Spanish.

photos.alt: Apple Mac mini M4 desktop computer photographed at an angle showing its front USB-C ports and the bottom face of the device, where the power button is hidden from normal view
photos.story: Apple's Mac mini M4 (launched late 2024) has its power button recessed on the underside of the device, requiring users to flip their computer upside-down to press it; Apple defended the choice saying users 'hardly ever' need the physical button, until macOS 26.5 added a keyboard shortcut workaround in May 2026.
photos.why_funny: Apple charged up to 1,399 USD for a desktop computer and hid the on/off button where no one can see or reach it without turning the whole machine upside-down — then justified this by saying nobody uses it anyway.

photos.alt: New 2026 Coca-Cola global brand refresh showing the redesigned red-and-white cans and bottles with the updated tall serif typeface that internet users compare to Marlboro cigarette packaging
photos.story: On July 20, 2026 Coca-Cola launched a global visual identity refresh — its new 'Better With' serif typeface is so similar to Marlboro's font that social media users immediately posted side-by-side comparisons, calling it the 'fridge cigarette' rebrand; simultaneously, swapping from black to white lettering makes Coke Zero nearly indistinguishable from regular Coke, alarming diabetics who rely on the colour difference.
photos.why_funny: The world's most iconic drink brand paid a branding agency millions to look 'more Coca-Cola' and accidentally arrived at 'more Marlboro' — while also making the safe-for-diabetics version of their drink invisible on the shelf.

photos.alt: Architectural rendering of the MUNA Quito competition-winning design — a massive pale concrete cube with irregularly-spaced rectangular window cutouts on its facade, set in a city block next to La Carolina Park with Quito's mountains visible in the background
photos.credit: Studio Campo Baeza / MAODA via ArchDaily
photos.story: Studio Campo Baeza and MAODA won an international competition to design Ecuador's new National Museum with 'Echoes of the Sun' — announced July 6, 2026 — but within days 20,000 Ecuadorians signed a petition comparing the concrete block to a cardboard box and DoodleBob from SpongeBob, the Vice Minister of Culture resigned, and the government 'recalled' the winning design.
photos.why_funny: 148 architecture teams from 20+ countries competed, an international expert jury crowned a winner, and Ecuador's public response was to circulate a petition calling the proposed national museum a SpongeBob character — and the government agreed.

photos.alt: Colorful Lollipop Star bone-conduction candy sticks displayed at CES 2026
photos.story: Lollipop Star debuted at CES 2026 as a single-use bone-conduction candy that beams celebrity songs through your jawbone to your inner ear, but only if you also wear earplugs to block ambient noise — after one session you throw away a plastic stick containing a lithium battery and a circuit board.
photos.why_funny: The 'Worst in Show' at CES 2026: you eat a $9 lollipop, plug your ears, and chew for music — the candy IS the speaker, the landfill IS the packaging.

photos.alt: Chromatic-aberration glitch effect on the AWS logo — the lowercase 'aws' lettering appears with yellow and blue colour-channel offsets against a dark grey background, with the familiar Amazon orange arrow-smile beneath
photos.story: Amazon Web Services' billing system confused gigabytes with bytes on July 17, 2026 — a 1-billion-fold unit conversion error — sending customers estimated bills as high as $7.1 trillion for accounts that normally owe pennies; AWS acknowledged the bug on social media with: 'Typo alert: Slight miscalculation on our end (very slight)'
photos.why_funny: The company trusted with running roughly a third of the internet's infrastructure made a CS101 bytes-vs-gigabytes mistake and invoiced one customer for more than twice Amazon's entire market cap.

photos.alt: Boston Dynamics' Atlas humanoid robot standing in an industrial promotional setting with Hyundai branding, the white and black bipedal robot looking both impressive and faintly ominous next to a Hyundai vehicle
photos.story: Hyundai deployed Boston Dynamics' Atlas robots to deliver the match ball at the FIFA World Cup on July 5 as a PR stunt, then 39,000 Hyundai factory workers launched the first-ever humanoid robot factory strike on July 13, demanding a say before Atlas enters their plants.
photos.why_funny: The same company that paid millions to showcase its human-replacement robots at the world's biggest sporting event triggered the first worker rebellion against those exact robots within two weeks.

photos.alt: Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google and Alphabet, on stage at the Google I/O developer conference at Moscone Center in San Francisco, presenting to a packed auditorium of developers with the Google I/O stage backdrop and lighting visible behind him
photos.story: Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro — announced at Google I/O in May 2026, with CEO Sundar Pichai telling a visibly frustrated crowd of developers 'Give us until next month to get it to you' — has since missed its promised June launch and its rescheduled July 17 target, making it the most publicly broken tech promise of the year.
photos.why_funny: The CEO of the world's most powerful search and AI infrastructure company promised his flagship model three times and missed all three, while rival models GPT-5.6 and Grok 4.5 already shipped.

photos.alt: Official POPOPO app promotional image showing two anime-style 3D avatar characters standing next to smartphones displaying video call screens, surrounded by floating cartoon mascots — a cat, panda, bear with a crown, and robot — against a bright blue background, with the POPOPO logo and Japanese text reading 'video calling without a camera'
photos.story: POPOPO — launched March 2026, backed by 4chan founder Hiroyuki, Evangelion director Hideaki Anno, and musician GACKT as 'the last human-made social network in the AI era' — announced its shutdown on July 15, 2026, only six months after launch, with the team stating 'we failed spectacularly.'
photos.why_funny: They declared war on AI with 'the last human social network,' then built an app where humans communicate exclusively through anime avatars called Holosuits, and it still collapsed in half a year.

photos.alt: Interior of AT&T Stadium in Arlington Texas glowing bright magenta-pink from rows of LED grow lights on suspended trusses above the soccer field, with the stands and giant video screens visible in the pink-lit darkness
photos.story: For the 2026 FIFA World Cup, AT&T Stadium hung 18 massive LED rigs from its ceiling and bathed the entire interior in magenta-pink light for months — because the retractable roof that makes the arena weather-proof also blocks the sunlight FIFA requires natural grass to have.
photos.why_funny: A $1.2 billion NFL stadium needed a full-scale indoor farm installation because the architects never considered that football grass and World Cup grass have one thing in common: they both need the sun.

photos.alt: A soccer referee crouching on the pitch to spray a white foam vanishing-spray line before a free kick, with players and a packed stadium visible behind him
photos.story: Referee Ivan Barton walked out to officiate the France vs Spain World Cup semi-final on July 15, 2026 without his vanishing spray, forcing the fourth official to sprint onto the pitch mid-free-kick to hand it to him.
photos.why_funny: The vanishing spray is the most referee-specific gadget at the tournament — and the referee forgot it at the biggest match of the year.

photos.alt: Editorial illustration showing the xAI logo on a black container ejecting code files and a red .env file showing API_KEY and DB_PASS credentials, flying via dotted lines to a locked cloud storage icon
photos.story: Security researchers revealed on July 13, 2026 that xAI's Grok Build CLI was silently uploading entire Git repositories — including .env files with API keys and passwords — to Google Cloud Storage without consent, sending 5.1GB when only 192KB was needed for its task. Disabling the privacy toggle changed nothing.
photos.why_funny: The tool sold as a coding helper was simultaneously acting as a codebase vacuum cleaner, slurping up every secret and credential in the repo and sending them to the cloud — 26,500 times more data than it actually needed.

photos.alt: Annotated diagram of the Trump International Airport eagle logo with arrows pointing out deformed mismatched talons, unequal wing feathers, and wrong number of shield stripes
photos.story: Palm Beach airport was renamed Donald J. Trump International Airport in July 2026, but the grand new welcome-sign logo appears to be AI-generated — the eagle has deformed talons of different shapes, wings with mismatched feather counts, and only 11 stripes on its shield instead of the correct 13.
photos.why_funny: They renamed an entire international airport and put a giant sign out front, then apparently asked an AI for the logo and didn't look too closely at the talons.

photos.alt: Screenshot of the ChatGPT Atlas browser interface, showing an AI-powered browser window with a ChatGPT sidebar alongside a standard web page
photos.story: OpenAI launched the Atlas browser in October 2025 promising to 'rethink the web itself' with AI at the core — and is shutting it down August 9, 2026, less than 9 months later, after executives decided it was a 'side quest' and folded its features into a Chrome extension instead.
photos.why_funny: They announced they were going to reinvent how all of humanity browses the internet, then quietly concluded the browser was basically a distraction and shipped a Chrome extension.

photos.alt: The Lepro Ami device on the CES 2026 show floor: a compact standing curved OLED display showing an animated AI avatar face, surrounded by trade show visitors
photos.credit: iFixit / Repair.org — Worst in Show CES 2026
photos.story: Lepro's 'Ami' — an always-on desktop device with dual cameras, eye-tracking, and AR marketed as an AI 'soulmate' for remote workers — was voted the People's Choice Worst in Show at CES 2026 and is now hitting shelves in July 2026.
photos.why_funny: They built a surveillance camera that watches you all day, called it your romantic companion, and the public immediately voted it the single worst product at the world's biggest tech show.

photos.alt: A small white cube-shaped device on a workbench being tested — it looks like a compact desktop fan, not an air conditioner
photos.story: Social-media ads for cheap 'portable air conditioners' — claiming NASA engineering and a 17°C room-drop in minutes — are going viral in the UK heatwave; a YouTuber who bought one found a small evaporative fan worth a few pounds; the ASA confirmed the claims are false and is banning the ads.
photos.why_funny: The product was marketed with AI-generated copper-coil imagery and fake customer reviews, but opens to reveal a tiny plastic box fan that can't meaningfully cool a closet.

photos.alt: Row of white Waymo autonomous robotaxis with sensor domes on their roofs, parked on a San Francisco city street
photos.story: On July 4, 2026, Waymo robotaxis drove directly into lit fireworks in San Francisco, gridlocked for hours as batteries ran out, and had to be towed — while the company's handful of remote operators couldn't unstick dozens of stalled cars at once.
photos.why_funny: The car designed to remove human error drove into explosives because there was no human to say 'maybe don't.'

photos.alt: Back view of a white Google Pixel smartphone showing the camera module and Google logo, the location of the Quick Tap gesture sensor that stops working when a phone case is applied
photos.story: Google's 'Quick Tap' feature lets Pixel owners double-tap the back of their phone to trigger shortcuts, but a July 7, 2026 Pocket-lint investigation found the sensor cannot reliably detect taps through even a thin silicone case — meaning the feature is functionally useless for the overwhelming majority of users who protect their phones.
photos.why_funny: Google engineered a time-saving shortcut for the imaginary Pixel owner who keeps their $1,000 phone naked, leaving everyone else to tap their way to absolutely nothing.

photos.alt: Buckled concrete slabs with rebar pushed upward across northbound lanes of Interstate 97 in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, after extreme July 4th heat caused the pavement to blow out
photos.story: On July 4th, 2026, record heat caused a concrete section of I-97 near Baltimore to buckle and thrust broken slabs and exposed rebar upward across all three northbound lanes; engineers note the road was designed to historical temperature specs that assumed modern July heat would never occur.
photos.why_funny: American infrastructure failed spectacularly on Independence Day because mid-20th century engineers built roads for a climate that no longer exists — and the fix takes six to nine hours on a holiday weekend.

photos.alt: The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington DC in June 2026 showing the newly painted blue floor with algae bloom and cleanup equipment visible on the pool edge following the controversial $14.6M renovation
photos.story: The Trump administration paid $14.6 million to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and paint the floor and walls 'American flag blue'; within weeks the polyurea coating was peeling off in large floating chunks, algae bloomed green, and when visitors touched the floating flakes Trump blamed 'vandals' and ordered arrests.
photos.why_funny: A renovation whose entire design premise was 'the pool should be blue' produced a pool that was blue for the wrong reasons — floating paint chips and algae — and the administration's response was to arrest tourists for touching the evidence.

photos.alt: Boeing's CST-100 Starliner spacecraft undocking from the International Space Station following its Crew Flight Test mission in 2024, floating in orbit with the Earth's limb visible below
photos.story: A NASA Inspector General report published July 1, 2026 formally expressed doubt that Boeing's CST-100 Starliner will ever achieve human-rating certification — after $4.8 billion spent, repeated helium leaks, propulsion failures, and unresolved parachute anomalies — explicitly citing 'overconfidence in Boeing's heritage systems' and 'unrealistic launch schedules' as root causes, with the ISS due to retire around 2030.
photos.why_funny: Boeing convinced NASA and Congress to fund a multi-decade space taxi entirely on the premise that their old aerospace skills were still reliable — the Inspector General's report is the official confirmation that they were not.

photos.alt: A phone screen showing the Kalshi prediction market app interface displaying bet options on streaming music outcomes, photographed in Chicago, Illinois
photos.credit: Scott Olson/Getty Images via Hollywood Reporter
photos.story: Kalshi launched a prediction market with $3M in trading volume betting on which song would be Spotify's most-streamed in June 2026; a trader then bought over 500,000 fake streams to push obscure artist Malcolm Todd's 'Earrings' to #1, collected the payout — and Spotify only removed the fraudulent streams after the market had already been settled and winners paid, exposing the fundamental design flaw in building a financial instrument on a metric any bettor can directly manipulate.
photos.why_funny: Kalshi spent months engineering a sophisticated prediction market on Spotify's chart data and apparently never considered that anyone with enough skin in the game could simply purchase a #1 for a fraction of the payout.

photos.alt: A PlayStation 5 disc-edition console displayed in a locked glass case at a Japanese electronics store, with the Sony logo and PlayStation 5 branding visible
photos.story: Sony announced on July 1, 2026 that physical disc production for all new PlayStation games will end in January 2028 — simultaneously with GTA 6 confirming that its $80 'physical edition' ships with only a download code in an empty cardboard box, with no disc ever planned.
photos.why_funny: They engineered a beautifully slotted disc drive into millions of consoles, then announced the slot is now purely decorative.

photos.alt: A black Skydio X10 quadcopter drone in flight against a clear blue sky, rotors spinning, seen from a low angle showing all four arms and propellers
photos.credit: Sgt. Austin Steinborn / U.S. Army (Wikimedia Commons)
photos.story: NYPD's Skydio X10 drone — marketed by Skydio as providing 'zero-failure security' with 'autonomous patrols at scale' — malfunctioned, fell from the sky, and caught fire near the FIFA World Cup Fan Zone entrance at Brooklyn Bridge Park on June 23, 2026, while thousands of fans were in the area; this is the second time the same NYPD drone model has caught fire.
photos.why_funny: A 'zero-failure' security drone achieved total failure in the most literal way possible — by crashing and burning right next to the event it was supposed to protect.

photos.alt: Side-by-side before/after comparison of photos processed by Sony Xperia AI Camera Assistant, showing the AI-enhanced right panel is noticeably washed out with reduced colour and contrast compared to the original
photos.story: Sony launched an AI Camera Assistant for the Xperia 1 VIII that supposedly improves your photos, then posted official before/after marketing shots where the AI-processed version was visibly washed out, overexposed and lower quality; Nothing CEO Carl Pei publicly asked 'This must be engagement farming?' and Sony had to quietly post new comparisons.
photos.why_funny: Sony ran a marketing campaign to prove their AI made photos better, accidentally proved the opposite, and had to reshoot their own proof.

photos.alt: Snap CEO Evan Spiegel wearing chunky oversized black Snap Specs AR glasses while being interviewed by TV camera at the 2026 Specs launch event, with 'SPECS' branding signage visible behind him
photos.story: Snap launched 'Specs' AR glasses on June 16, 2026 at $2,195 — CEO Evan Spiegel described them as 'highly wearable' at the launch event in footage that visibly shows the 136-gram chunky frames flattening his earlobes, the company's top Specs exec had already quit, and Snap stock fell ~10% on launch day.
photos.why_funny: The CEO used himself as a live product demo to prove wearability and simultaneously demonstrated the opposite, on camera, at the launch event.

photos.alt: Close-up of the dark grey underside of an Apple Mac mini M4, showing the circular ventilation grille and a power button symbol tucked in the corner, photographed from below against a blue background
photos.story: Apple's M4 Mac mini (launched late 2024) placed the power button on the underside of the device; after 18 months of mockery, Apple 'fixed' this in macOS 26.5 with a Power Control software feature — and the official release notes admit users may 'not have easy access to the computer's power button.'
photos.why_funny: Apple's answer to 'we put the power button where no one can reach it' was to ship a software update so you can avoid ever touching the power button — rather than move the button.

photos.alt: Modern Samsung 4-door white refrigerator with no handle, flush with wood-paneled kitchen cabinetry, small touchscreen displaying abstract art where a door handle would normally be
photos.story: Samsung's 2026 Bespoke AI Family Hub refrigerator removes the physical handle entirely, requiring voice commands or palm-tapping a sensor to open it; consumer groups named it 'Worst in Show' at CES 2026, and BGR named it a top disappointment of the year in June 2026, noting that if you lose internet you also lose the ability to open your fridge.
photos.why_funny: A $3,500 appliance whose designers solved the humble handle problem by requiring a stable broadband connection to access your own leftover pizza.

photos.alt: Dark navy blue Steam Machine gaming PC cube sitting on a wood desk next to a monitor showing a colorful game, with two small decorative mushroom figurines beside it
photos.story: The $1,049 Valve Steam Machine launched June 22, 2026 with '4K gaming at 60 FPS' prominently on its store page; after reviews showed most AAA games couldn't hit that target even on medium settings, Valve silently changed the claim to 'up to 4K gaming with FSR 4.1' on June 25.
photos.why_funny: Valve spent years over-promising 4K 60fps performance and, when reviewers proved it wrong in real games, solved the controversy by just deleting the claim from the store page.

photos.alt: Montana Highway Patrol trooper standing beside a 23-foot bright yellow fiberglass banana-shaped car pulled over on the shoulder of Interstate 90 near Billings
photos.story: Steve Braithwaite's Big Banana Car — a 23-foot fiberglass banana mounted on a 1993 Ford F-150 — was pulled over again on I-90 near Billings, Montana on June 24, 2026 because cargo boxes partially blocked his 'SPLIT' license plate, continuing a 15-year tradition: he says he was 'the most pulled-over man in America' for the first eight years of driving it.
photos.why_funny: He built a vehicle specifically designed to look like a giant banana, expected to drive it legally across America, and is still surprised it keeps attracting police attention — the banana shape physically prevents proper license plate display.

photos.alt: Google Home Speaker in Jade green with rainbow LED touch-control lights at its base and a white USB-C power cable permanently exiting from the lower-back of the unit with no visible port to disconnect it
photos.story: The Google Home Speaker, Google's first new smart speaker in six years, launched June 25, 2026 with a permanently attached USB-C power cable — there is no port on the device, so if the cable (the most fragile component) breaks, the $99 speaker cannot be repaired without opening the case.
photos.why_funny: Six years of development time and not a single engineer added a cable port — every previous Google speaker had a removable cord, making this the first that turns a frayed cable into a landfill trip.

photos.alt: Scotland players in dark navy jerseys clustered at the touchline taking water bottles during an official hydration break in their 2026 World Cup match against Morocco
photos.story: FIFA introduced mandatory three-minute 'hydration breaks' in all 2026 World Cup matches, insisting they're for player welfare — but they stop play even in 19°C/66°F rainy Toronto, air-conditioned Dallas, and indoor Atlanta, while Fox Sports airs full-screen commercials during every pause.
photos.why_funny: FIFA designed a player-welfare break that triggers in cold, wet, air-conditioned stadiums where the only thing being refreshed is Fox's $200,000-per-slot ad revenue — and every fan in every stadium boos it.

photos.alt: Four NASA astronauts floating in zero gravity on the International Space Station, kicking and passing the official FIFA World Cup 2026 Trionda ball between them, with national flags visible on the wall behind
photos.license: editorial — © Gulf News (NASA imagery not copyrighted)
photos.story: Adidas designed the Trionda with a 500Hz sensor chip, deep seams, and fluid geometry — producing a ball so aerodynamically unpredictable that it has caused 19 goalkeeper errors in the tournament's opening weeks (nearly the same as all of Qatar 2022), while NASA simultaneously took one to the ISS to study why it behaves so oddly.
photos.why_funny: Adidas over-engineered a round ball so thoroughly that it baffled both the world's best goalkeepers and the world's best physicists at the exact same time.

photos.alt: AT&T Stadium interior entirely bathed in pink-purple glow from 18 LED grow lights suspended above a green grass soccer field
photos.story: AT&T Stadium — a billion-dollar indoor NFL dome in Arlington, Texas — installed 18 pink LED grow lights suspended from the ceiling and shipped Colorado-grown grass 800 miles to North Texas, raising the entire playing surface 24 inches above the concrete floor, all because FIFA insists on natural turf for World Cup matches.
photos.why_funny: They built a magnificent roofed stadium and then had to construct a full-scale greenhouse inside it to host a sport that normally happens outdoors.

photos.alt: Ground crew workers with buckets and tools mopping water from the waterlogged Gillette Stadium pitch after a sprinkler flooded Iraq's penalty box during halftime of the Norway vs Iraq FIFA World Cup 2026 match
photos.story: During halftime of Norway vs Iraq at Gillette Stadium (June 16, 2026), a sprinkler erupted in Iraq's penalty box and flooded the pitch; ground crew rushed in with buckets while Norway's coach simultaneously complained the grass was 'tinder dry.'
photos.why_funny: The irrigation system at a FIFA World Cup venue managed to both drown one end of the pitch and leave the other parched — at the same time.

photos.alt: New Shrek 5 animation still showing Shrek with a stunned expression, featuring the controversial redesigned softer, rounder character style with larger eyes
photos.story: The Shrek 5 trailer dropped June 16, 2026, revealing redesigned characters with softer contours and Disney-large eyes — sparking such fierce backlash (#NotMyShrek, comparisons to 'AI slop') that Universal disabled YouTube comments entirely.
photos.why_funny: A studio spent years redesigning an ogre who was already perfectly ugly, made him look like a knockoff Disney sidekick, then silenced everyone who noticed.

photos.alt: France's Kylian Mbappé stretching to reach the ball on the bright green Bermuda grass pitch at MetLife Stadium during the France vs Senegal World Cup Group I match on 16 June 2026
photos.story: After seven years of engineering research, FIFA installed Tahoma 31 Bermudagrass at MetLife Stadium — the World Cup Final venue — but France coach Deschamps said it 'might be cement below the grass,' midfielder Rabiot called it 'more like an artificial surface,' and Brazil's Vinicius said it dries out so fast the ball slows mid-game.
photos.why_funny: Seven years and millions of dollars of sports-science turf research produced a field the world's best players refuse to wear studs on.

photos.alt: Aerial photo of Switzerland's World Cup training pitch in San Diego with a bold red overlay on the canyon hillside behind it reading 'SNAKE AREA' in large white text
photos.story: Switzerland's FIFA-approved 2026 World Cup training base at San Diego Jewish Academy required the Swiss Football Association to mark a red 'SNAKE AREA' on their official facility map — because four species of venomous rattlesnakes inhabit the California canyon behind the pitch.
photos.why_funny: FIFA planned a World Cup across North America without checking whether 'no venomous wildlife on the training pitch' was a reasonable expectation, forcing Switzerland to publish an official snake-exclusion zone as part of their training-camp layout.

photos.alt: The exterior of Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara showing the iconic red batwing logo tightly wrapped in a white tarp, the distinctive two-wing silhouette still clearly visible through the covering despite FIFA's clean-venue rules
photos.story: FIFA's 'clean venue' rule forced Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara to wrap its iconic batwing logo in a white tarp for the World Cup — but the tarp preserved the logo's distinctive silhouette so perfectly that the covered version went viral worldwide, becoming more recognisable than the original.
photos.why_funny: A rule designed to erase a brand from billions of TV screens instead turned that brand into the most-discussed logo at the tournament — Levi's even swapped their Instagram profile picture to the covered version.

photos.alt: Three Scotland football fans in national-team jerseys smiling in front of a bright yellow 'SCHOOL BUS' — part of a fan-organised fleet of 20 school buses used to transport 1,100 Tartan Army supporters to Gillette Stadium for the 2026 World Cup
photos.story: Scotland fans organised a fleet of 20 yellow school buses to reach Gillette Stadium for the 2026 World Cup after official FIFA shuttles charged $80–95 round-trip — versus the fans' self-organised rate of $38 — because the US public transit system offers no viable route to the venue.
photos.why_funny: Scotland returned to the World Cup for the first time in 28 years only to discover that the host nation's infrastructure is so inadequate that fan volunteers had to charter almost every school bus in Rhode Island to watch the match.

photos.alt: A large alligator resting on the edge of a cart path at ChampionGates golf course in Florida, half on the path and half on the fairway grass, with a pond visible in the background
photos.story: Multiple Portugal World Cup players refused to leave their hotel rooms at their FIFA-approved Palm Beach Gardens, Florida training camp after 3–4 alligators were spotted roaming near the practice fields and adjacent lake on June 14, 2026.
photos.why_funny: FIFA approved a World Cup training facility where prehistoric reptiles patrol the grounds — and the world's best footballers are too scared to go to training.

photos.alt: Close-up of a dark blue paramedic uniform bearing a badge reading 'ALTA PARAMEDIC HEALTH' with a generic corporate mountain logo
photos.story: Alberta secretly rebranded its 3,500-paramedic Emergency Health Services to 'Alta Paramedic Health' — spending $25,000 on prototypes without telling any staff — until the Health Minister personally ordered it stopped after a wave of public backlash.
photos.why_funny: The new badge looks indistinguishable from a supplement brand or yoga studio, which is exactly the wrong vibe for the people you're calling at 3am.

photos.alt: Crowd of World Cup fans in USA jerseys queuing at a large blue FIFA 'Gate C / Workforce & Volunteer Entrance' sign at Los Angeles Stadium
photos.story: FIFA's Los Angeles Stadium opened Gate C with no public-facing signage, sending thousands of ticketed fans into a queue at a 'Workforce & Volunteer Entrance' that turned them away — then forced a half-mile walk around the stadium to find the actual public gate.
photos.why_funny: The gate that thousands lined up for was, specifically, the one not for them — announced on a sign they apparently did not read until they were already in the queue.

photos.alt: Aerial Google Maps view of Telford Drive in Slough showing a painted bike lane where the white bicycle symbol stencilled on the road is visibly wider than the lane boundary lines on either side
photos.story: Slough Borough Council installed a painted advisory bike lane on Telford Drive so narrow that the bicycle symbol stencilled on it overflows both edges of the lane — cyclists noted it would 'fail to meet the minimum handlebar width for the UCI.'
photos.why_funny: The road marking that is supposed to mark the space for cyclists is physically larger than the space itself — a bike lane that cannot fit a bicycle.

photos.alt: Hotel front-desk receptionist and guest both stare at a Philips dual-sided monitor sitting between them on the counter, neither looking at the other
photos.story: Philips launched the world's first 'dual-sided' business monitor so two people can share a screen in a face-to-face meeting — critics immediately noted the flaw: placing a screen between two people to help them look at each other ensures neither one does.
photos.why_funny: The device invented to improve 'face-to-face collaboration' is a screen you put between two faces so they stop looking at each other.

photos.alt: Four-panel photo of Brazil soccer players at the 2026 World Cup wearing Nike jerseys with visibly stiff, protruding shoulder seams that jut outward like armored pauldrons instead of draping naturally
photos.story: Nike's high-tech Aero-FIT jerseys for the 2026 World Cup have overly wide, stiffened shoulder seams that refuse to drape flat, making players look like they're wearing Shredder's armor from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles — and Nike admitted the flaw but still hasn't fixed it.
photos.why_funny: A $200 shirt designed to make elite athletes look faster instead makes them look like a cartoon villain.

photos.alt: Back of the gold Trump Mobile T1 smartphone showing an American flag etched into the casing with only 11 stripes instead of the correct 13, above the 'TRUMP MOBILE' wordmark
photos.story: The $499 Trump Mobile T1 phone, promoted as a patriotic 'Made in USA' device, shipped in May 2026 as a rebranded HTC handset made in China — with an American flag etched on the back that has only 11 stripes instead of the correct 13.
photos.why_funny: A phone whose entire identity is American patriotism couldn't get the flag right, and wasn't even made in America.

photos.alt: Three cans of 'Good Nut' organic coconut water — Tom Brady's new beverage brand — displayed side by side in original, chocolate, and sparkling varieties
photos.story: Tom Brady launched an organic coconut water brand called 'Good Nut' via Gopuff on June 8, 2026 — going to such elaborate lengths to avoid saying the product's own name in the launch video that he stops himself every time he's about to say it, even though the cans were already printed.
photos.why_funny: A seven-time Super Bowl champion named his health drink 'Good Nut,' filmed a whole ad where he refuses to say its name, and shipped the cans anyway.

photos.alt: Official NEOM concept render showing two impossibly tall mirrored walls stretching along the Saudi Red Sea coast to the horizon — the planned 170km 'The Line' megacity
photos.story: Saudi Arabia's NEOM halted construction of 'The Line' — a planned 170km mirrored-wall city for 9 million people — after completing just 2.4km of foundation (1.4%), delaying the project until at least 2030 as internal audits put the true cost near $9 trillion.
photos.why_funny: They unveiled billion-dollar CGI of a 170km city for 9 million and physically built less than a kilometre and a half of it.

photos.alt: Aerial view of the Mira-Bhayandar double-decker flyover near Mumbai, showing a wide 4-lane approach road abruptly funnelling into a thin 2-lane bridge over the city
photos.story: A brand-new Mumbai Metro Line 9 double-decker flyover in Mira-Bhayandar went viral in January 2026 when aerial footage showed its four-lane stretch abruptly narrowing to two lanes — and the road authority's official response was that it was 'planned' and 'not a design flaw.'
photos.why_funny: They built half the bridge and called it a feature.

photos.alt: Apple promotional image showing a Mac, iPad, iPhone, and Apple Watch all running iOS 26's Liquid Glass interface — a translucent, blurry UI redesign so unpopular Apple is adding a slider to turn it off
photos.story: Apple's 'Liquid Glass' redesign in iOS 26 was so roundly rejected that only 15% of iPhone users upgraded (vs 63% for iOS 18), and at WWDC 2026 this week Apple is quietly announcing a system-wide slider so users can dial down — or off — their own flagship design.
photos.why_funny: Apple spent years building a translucent UI so beautiful it needs a dimmer switch to make it usable.

photos.alt: A yellow diamond road warning sign in New South Wales whose arrows are so tangled and looping that the road layout it depicts is impossible to understand, with a baffled man pointing up at it
photos.story: A road sign meant to warn drivers about an upcoming junction is drawn with so many tangled, looping arrows that it conveys nothing except confusion.
photos.why_funny: The one job of a warning sign is to be understood at a glance — this one needs a warning sign of its own.

photos.alt: Screenshot of Amazon Shopping app search bar showing AI-generated images of non-existent clothing products while the user types a search query
photos.story: Amazon's Shopping app now generates AI images of clothes and furniture that don't exist while you type a search query, to 'help' you find real products on a site that already has millions of real product photos.
photos.why_funny: The world's largest product catalog decided the best way to help shoppers find real things is to first show them fake things — for some reason.

photos.alt: The Estadio Azteca (Estadio Banorte) in Mexico City, a 2026 FIFA World Cup venue, seen from the stands
photos.story: FIFA's World Cup 2026 ticketing site accidentally sold about 60 fans tickets for $0, then cancelled them and told the fans to buy the same seats again at full price.
photos.why_funny: The most lucrative World Cup ever, projected to make $11bn, built a checkout that gave seats away for free and then demanded the money back.

photos.alt: An Apple Magic Mouse flipped on its back to charge, with the cable plugging into the underside so it cannot be used while charging
photos.story: Apple put the charging port on the bottom of the Magic Mouse, so it lies belly-up and unusable while it charges.
photos.why_funny: A premium mouse that has to flip over and play dead to charge — designed with a flaw nobody could miss.
